vignette:
The Weight of the Intersection

Maya is twenty-one years old and works as an apprentice electrician for a commercial contractor in a mid-sized city in the Pacific Northwest. She is the kind of young woman who has always been comfortable with her hands - precise, patient, unafraid of tight spaces or heights. Her coworkers describe her as steady. She used to think of herself that way too.

Fourteen months ago, Maya was driving home from a job site on a Thursday evening, still in her work boots and hi-vis vest, when a pickup truck ran a red light at highway speed and struck the driver's side of her car. The impact spun her vehicle across two lanes. She remembers the sound - a sound she says is impossible to describe to anyone who hasn't heard it - and then she remembers looking down at her left hand, which was pressed against the shattered window, and thinking with strange calm that she could not feel it. She was conscious throughout. It took forty minutes for the fire crew to cut her out. She spent three days in hospital with a fractured clavicle, lacerations to her face and forearm, and a mild traumatic brain injury. The driver of the truck was uninjured. He had run the light because he was looking at his phone.

In the weeks after the accident, Maya told herself she was fine. She went back to work as soon as her clavicle allowed, reasoning that being useful would help. And for a while, being on a job site - the noise, the tasks, the company of her crew - did seem to dull something. But the drive to work became its own ordeal. She began taking longer routes to avoid the intersection where the crash happened. Then she started avoiding intersections with traffic lights altogether, which in a city is nearly impossible. She now carpools with a coworker whenever she can, offering to cover his coffee and lunch without explaining why.

At night, Maya sleeps poorly. She wakes between two and four in the morning with her heart already racing, sometimes mid-scream, sometimes just sitting bolt upright in the dark with the absolute certainty that something is wrong. The dreams are not always about the crash directly - sometimes she is simply trapped somewhere and cannot move her hand. She has stopped mentioning the nightmares to her mother, who lives two hours away, because she does not want to be told to see someone.

During the day, the intrusions come without warning. The sound of a car braking hard on the street below her apartment sends a cold wave through her chest that takes minutes to settle. A coworker dropped a conduit last month and Maya found herself against the far wall of the room before she had any conscious awareness of moving. She laughed it off. She is good at laughing things off.

What Maya finds harder to laugh off is the numbness she has noticed in herself over the past several months. She used to go out on weekends with friends from her trade program. She has declined so many invitations now that most of them have stopped asking. She sits with her back to walls in restaurants when she does go out, scanning exits, unable to follow conversations because part of her attention is always somewhere else - listening, watching, waiting for something she cannot name. She describes feeling like she is watching her own life from a slight distance, as though there is a pane of glass between her and everything that used to feel ordinary.

What brought her in, finally, was a moment on a job site last week. She was running conduit near a loading bay when a delivery truck pulled in fast. She froze completely - hands at her sides, unable to move or speak for what she estimates was about thirty seconds. A colleague asked if she was alright. She said yes. That evening, she made the appointment.

She sits in the chair across from the desk with her work-calloused hands folded in her lap, and she says she just wants to feel like herself again.
